Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write the vision section of an internal engineering strategy document about investing in platform work over the next two years. Around 250 words.

Platform work is the code that lets every other team move faster without thinking about it: build systems, shared libraries, deployment pipelines, internal tooling, data infrastructure. Over the past two years we treated it as overhead and funded it with whatever engineers had spare time. Builds are slow, services are duplicated, and onboarding takes weeks instead of days.

Over the next two years we will staff platform work with a dedicated team, give it its own roadmap, and hold it to the same planning rigor as product features. Every project on this roadmap ties to a measurable outcome: build time, deploy frequency, incident recovery time, or the number of teams able to ship without platform help.

This will feel slower before it feels faster. Migrating services onto shared infrastructure, retiring one-off tools, and consolidating deployment paths will pull engineers off feature work for a quarter or two.

That cost is real. We accept it because the alternative costs more: every team rebuilds the same primitives, debugs the same class of production issues, and onboards new hires against inconsistent systems. We already pay that cost; it just doesn't show up on a roadmap.

By the end of this period, a new engineer ships their first change in under a week. A team building a new service reaches for existing infrastructure by default, not because someone told them to, but because it's faster than building their own. That's what this investment is for.

The text above has these problems. Rewrite it so none remain.
Change nothing else, and keep the same length and purpose.

- paragraph_uniformity (5 paragraphs, spread 0.23):

Return only the rewritten text.
